client.name: Al Noor Mini Market
client.profile: A small corner grocery near the bank's branch. Abu Salem has banked with us for years — deposits his takings every evening. First time asking for financing.

request: "Ramadan is coming and I want to fill the shop with stock — juices, dates, rice. I need about KD 20,000. I'll sell it all during the season and pay you back from the sales. Can the bank help?"

figures.label: How long until he can repay

ratios.label: The key question
ratios.hint: Every loan needs a repayment source — the cash that will pay it back. Here it's the Ramadan sales: he buys stock, sells it, and the sales money repays the bank. This is the first question a banker asks about ANY financing.

ratios.label: Does the story add up?
ratios.hint: His Ramadan sales jump by KD 17,000 a month. Over the season that's far more than KD 20,000 — so the repayment source is realistic.

decisions.prompt: First lesson: every financing needs a repayment source. What repays this loan?

options.label: The Ramadan sales — he turns the stock into cash and pays us from that
options.feedback: Exactly. The stock becomes sales, the sales become cash, the cash repays the loan. When a banker can trace that path clearly, the loan makes sense. This path is called the repayment source.

options.label: His house — if he doesn't pay we take it
options.feedback: That's collateral (a backup if things go wrong), not a repayment source. Banks lend against the cash a business will generate — security is the safety net, never the plan.

options.label: He seems trustworthy — that's enough
options.feedback: Trust matters, but trust doesn't transfer money. Without a clear answer to 'where will the cash come from?', there is no loan — however honest the client.

options.label: The bank's profits cover it if he can't pay
options.feedback: If the bank planned to absorb losses, it would be a charity. Every dinar lent must have a planned way home.

decisions.prompt: Now choose the financing. He needs KD 20,000 for about 3 months.

options.label: A short-term loan, repaid after the season — about 3 months
options.feedback: The loan's length matches the need: 3 months of stock, 3 months of financing. Matching the loan to the need is one of the most important habits in banking.

options.label: A 10-year loan — give him plenty of time
options.feedback: He'd be paying interest for 10 years on stock he sold in 3 months. Longer is not kinder — it's just more expensive. Match the financing to the need.

options.label: KD 100,000 — take extra just in case
options.feedback: Five times what he needs. Extra borrowed money doesn't sit still — it gets spent, and then it must be repaid from sales that were only ever going to cover KD 20,000.

options.label: No loan — tell him to save up for a few years
options.feedback: Financing exactly this kind of short, self-repaying need is what banks are for. The season won't wait for savings.

learn: Every financing starts with one question: where will repayment come from? Trace the path from the money's use to the cash that brings it back — and match the loan's length to that path.

client.name: Bin Daij Electronics
client.profile: Sells phones and accessories in a busy mall. Healthy little business — this visit is about timing, not trouble.

request: "Here's my problem: salaries go out on the 25th of every month, but the mall pays me my card sales on the 5th. For about ten days a month I'm short maybe KD 8,000 — then the money arrives and I'm fine again. What do I do?"

ratios.label: What kind of need is this?
ratios.value: A timing gap, not missing money
ratios.hint: Yaqoub isn't short of money — his money arrives ten days late. The business is fine; only the calendar is awkward. Banks have a special tool for exactly this.

ratios.label: The tool
ratios.hint: An overdraft lets his account dip below zero up to an agreed limit. He pays interest only on the days he actually uses it — perfect for a gap that opens and closes by itself.

decisions.prompt: What fits a 10-day gap that closes by itself every month?

options.label: An overdraft — the account can dip to −KD 10,000 and recovers when the mall pays
options.feedback: The overdraft is built for exactly this: short dips that fix themselves. He pays interest only for the days he's below zero — maybe ten days a month.

options.label: A KD 10,000 loan for 5 years
options.feedback: He'd carry debt for five years — and pay five years of interest — to cover a gap that lasts ten days. The size of the tool must match the size of the problem.

options.label: Tell him to delay salaries to the 5th
options.feedback: Solving the bank's puzzle by making his staff wait for wages is no solution at all — and likely illegal. Banks exist to bridge exactly these gaps.

options.label: A KD 50,000 credit line — room to grow
options.feedback: Six times the need. Unused limits tempt unplanned spending, and the bank carries risk it was never asked to carry. Size to the need.

decisions.prompt: A month later you review his account. What does a HEALTHY overdraft look like?

options.label: It dips below zero mid-month and comes back above zero when the mall pays
options.feedback: That swing — down and back up — is the signature of a healthy overdraft. The account 'breathes'. The day it stops coming back up, something has changed in the business.

options.label: It stays at the bottom of the limit all month — he's getting full value
options.feedback: An overdraft that's always at its limit isn't breathing — it's stuck. That means the money went into something permanent, and a permanent need should never live on an overdraft.

options.label: It's never used at all — that's safest
options.feedback: Safe for the bank, but if he never needed it, we solved a problem he didn't have. A good facility gets used — correctly.

options.label: Doesn't matter, as long as interest is paid
options.feedback: Interest payments can hide a stuck account for months. Bankers read the pattern of the account, not just the interest line.

learn: An overdraft covers short gaps that close by themselves — the account should swing below zero and back. An overdraft that's always full is a warning sign: permanent money is hiding in a temporary tool.

client.name: Deema Furniture House
client.profile: Imports sofas from a factory in Turkey she found online. First import deal of this size — and she's nervous.

request: "The Turkish factory wants KD 30,000 before they ship anything. I've never met them! If I send the money and no sofas arrive, I'm finished. But they say they won't make the furniture without guaranteed payment. We're stuck — can the bank fix this?"

figures.label: The deadlock
figures.value: She won't pay first; they won't ship first

ratios.label: The problem in one word
ratios.hint: Neither side wants to move first. This exact problem is centuries old — and banks invented a tool for it: the Letter of Credit (LC).

ratios.label: How the LC works
ratios.value: The bank promises the seller: 'ship the goods, show us the shipping documents, and WE pay you'
ratios.hint: The seller trusts the bank even if they don't trust Deema. And Deema's money only moves when documents prove the sofas were actually shipped. Both sides are protected.

decisions.prompt: Two strangers, neither willing to move first. What does the bank offer?

options.label: A Letter of Credit — the bank pays the factory when shipping documents prove the sofas are on the way
options.feedback: This is the LC's whole purpose: the factory trusts the bank's promise, and Deema's money moves only against proof of shipment. The deadlock dissolves.

options.label: Lend her KD 30,000 to wire in advance
options.feedback: Now it's the bank's money on a one-way trip to a stranger's account. If nothing ships, the loss is just bigger and better funded. The risk wasn't money — it was trust.

options.label: Tell her to fly to Turkey and pay cash in person
options.feedback: Charming, expensive, and it still doesn't protect her — cash handed over is cash gone, whatever happens at the factory afterwards.

options.label: Advise her to find a local supplier instead
options.feedback: Telling clients to abandon good business because trust is hard is giving up — solving exactly this is what trade finance exists for.

decisions.prompt: Quick check — when does the bank actually pay the Turkish factory?

options.label: When the factory presents documents proving the goods were shipped as agreed
options.feedback: Correct — the LC pays against documents: a transport document, an invoice, a packing list matching the agreed terms. Paper proof first, payment second.

options.label: As soon as the LC is opened
options.feedback: That would just be a prepayment with extra steps. The protection IS the condition: no shipping documents, no payment.

options.label: After Deema sells the sofas
options.feedback: The factory would never accept terms tied to how well Deema's shop does. The LC pays on shipment, not on her sales.

options.label: Whenever the factory phones and asks politely
options.feedback: Banks pay against documents, not phone calls. The strictness is the safety.

learn: The Letter of Credit solves the oldest problem in trade: two strangers, neither willing to move first. The bank's promise replaces personal trust — and money moves only against documents proving shipment.

client.name: Hamdan Cleaning Services
client.profile: Cleans office buildings with a crew of 40. Wants to bid for his first government contract.

request: "The Ministry tender says every bidder must submit a 'bank guarantee of KD 5,000' with their offer. I don't want to borrow KD 5,000 — I just need this paper from the bank. What exactly are they asking for?"

ratios.label: Two families of facilities
ratios.hint: CASH facilities move money now (loans, overdrafts). NON-CASH facilities are promises — the bank guarantees something, and money only moves if a specific thing goes wrong. Hamdan needs a promise, not money.

ratios.label: This promise's name
ratios.hint: It tells the Ministry: 'if this bidder wins and then walks away, the bank pays you KD 5,000.' It keeps bidders serious — and it costs Hamdan a small fee, not a debt.

decisions.prompt: What is the Ministry actually asking Hamdan for?

options.label: A bank promise (a bid bond) — money only moves if he wins and then abandons his bid
options.feedback: Exactly — a non-cash facility. The bank lends its trustworthiness, not its money. Hamdan pays a small fee; no loan, no interest, no debt.

options.label: A KD 5,000 loan to deposit with the Ministry
options.feedback: The tender asks for a guarantee precisely so bidders DON'T have to park cash. Borrowing to deposit money defeats the whole design.

options.label: Proof he has KD 5,000 in his account
options.feedback: A balance today proves nothing about Thursday. The Ministry wants an enforceable promise from a bank, not a snapshot.

options.label: KD 5,000 in cash, in an envelope, handed to the tender committee
options.feedback: That's not a guarantee — depending on the envelope, it might be a bribe. Government tenders run on bank instruments for good reason.

decisions.prompt: Before issuing even this small promise, what should the bank ask itself?

options.label: If Hamdan wins, can he actually DO this contract? The bid bond is step one of a bigger relationship
options.feedback: Sharp thinking. If he wins, he'll be back for a bigger guarantee (a performance bond) and maybe financing. The bank should only help him bid for work he can genuinely deliver.

options.label: Nothing — it's only KD 5,000
options.feedback: Small guarantees lead to large ones. Issuing the bid bond signals the bank believes he can perform — believe it before you sign it.

options.label: Whether the Ministry is good for the money
options.feedback: Backwards — the Ministry RECEIVES the guarantee. The risk the bank carries is Hamdan's behaviour, not the Ministry's.

options.label: Whether to charge him interest on the KD 5,000
options.feedback: No money has moved, so there's nothing to charge interest on. Guarantees earn a fee — interest belongs to loans.

learn: Banking has two families: CASH facilities move money now (loans, overdrafts); NON-CASH facilities are promises (guarantees, LCs) where money moves only if something specific happens. A bid bond is a promise that keeps bidders serious.

client.name: Lulwa's Bakery
client.profile: Famous for her saffron cakes. The shop can't keep up with orders — she wants a second industrial oven.

request: "The oven costs KD 24,000 and will let me double my baking. I make about KD 1,000 profit a month now, and the supplier says the new oven should roughly double that. How should I pay for it?"

ratios.label: What kind of purchase is this?
ratios.hint: The oven isn't stock to resell — it's equipment she'll use for ten years. Long-lived assets are financed with LONG loans (term loans), repaid bit by bit from the profit the asset itself creates.

ratios.label: Can she afford the repayments?
ratios.hint: Pre-computed for you: a 3-year loan costs about KD 700 a month. Her profit after the new oven should be ~KD 2,000 — so repayments fit comfortably, with room if the forecast disappoints.

decisions.prompt: How should a 10-year oven be financed?

options.label: A term loan over ~3 years — monthly repayments from the extra profit the oven makes
options.feedback: The classic equipment loan: the asset works for years, so it's repaid over years — by the very profits it generates. The numbers show comfortable room.

options.label: Her overdraft — just let the account go down by KD 24,000
options.feedback: Remember Yaqoub's lesson? An overdraft is for gaps that close in days. An oven would sit on the overdraft for YEARS, jammed at the limit — the classic mismatch.

options.label: A 3-month loan — get it over with quickly
options.feedback: KD 8,000 a month against KD 2,000 of profit. The repayment schedule would crush the bakery the oven was meant to grow.

options.label: A Letter of Credit
options.feedback: An LC solves the trust problem in trade — it doesn't answer how the oven gets PAID FOR over time. (If the oven came from abroad, she might use both: LC to buy safely, term loan to repay.)

decisions.prompt: The golden rule hiding in this case — which is it?

options.label: Match the loan to the life of what it pays for: short needs, short loans; long assets, longer loans
options.feedback: That's the rule — bankers call a violation of it a 'maturity mismatch'. Stock for a season = months. An oven for a decade = years. The financing should mirror the thing financed.

options.label: Always pick whatever's cheapest this month
options.feedback: The overdraft might look 'cheap' until it's jammed for three years. Fit first, price second.

options.label: Never borrow for equipment — save up instead
options.feedback: Waiting two years to save KD 24,000 means two years of lost orders. Borrowing against an asset's own future profit is healthy finance, not recklessness.

options.label: The longer the loan, the better — small payments forever
options.feedback: A 20-year loan on a 10-year oven means a decade of paying for a machine that no longer exists. Long, yes — longer than the asset, never.

learn: Match the financing to the thing financed: short-lived needs take short facilities, long-lived assets take term loans — repaid over time by the profit the asset itself produces.

client.name: Jassim Auto Garage
client.profile: Busy workshop, good reputation. Asking for a KD 15,000 loan for new diagnostic equipment — and puzzled by one of the bank's questions.

request: "Your colleague asked me what 'security' I can offer for the loan. Security? I'm not hiding anything! What does the bank mean — and why isn't my word enough?"

ratios.label: What 'security' means
ratios.hint: Security (collateral) is something of value the bank can claim IF repayment fails: the equipment itself, a guarantee from the owner, a deposit. The plan is still his profits — security is the seatbelt, not the engine.

ratios.label: The fit rule
ratios.hint: For a KD 15,000 equipment loan: a claim over the equipment plus the owner's personal promise is proportionate. Demanding his family home would be absurd — and asking for nothing would be careless.

decisions.prompt: Explain it to Jassim: why does the bank ask for security even when it trusts him?

options.label: Because the future is uncertain for everyone — security protects the depositors' money if life surprises us
options.feedback: Well put. The money banks lend belongs to depositors. Security isn't suspicion — it's the discipline of protecting other people's money against surprises nobody plans.

options.label: Because the bank assumes every client will try to escape
options.feedback: If the bank truly believed that, it wouldn't lend at all. Security guards against misfortune more often than mischief — say it that way and clients understand.

options.label: It's just paperwork tradition — sign and ignore it
options.feedback: Security documents get exercised in real defaults to recover real money. Calling them decoration misleads the client and embarrasses the bank later.

options.label: Because rules are rules
options.feedback: True and useless. A banker who can't explain WHY a rule exists will never earn a client's confidence in it.

decisions.prompt: Now choose proportionate security for the KD 15,000 equipment loan.

options.label: A claim over the new equipment + Jassim's personal guarantee
options.feedback: Proportionate and natural: the financed asset backs its own loan, and his personal promise keeps him committed. This pattern repeats across all of banking.

options.label: A mortgage over his family home
options.feedback: For KD 15,000? Heavy, slow, expensive to register — and it tells a good client you see him as a risk. Proportionality is part of the craft.

options.label: Nothing — his word and a handshake
options.feedback: Friendly, but you've left depositors' money resting on luck. Easy, proportionate security exists — take it.

options.label: KD 15,000 cash held at the bank as deposit
options.feedback: If he had KD 15,000 spare, he wouldn't need the loan. Demanding cash to lend cash is a refusal wearing a smile.

facilitySummary: Equipment loan KD 15,000 (secured by equipment + PG)
learn: Security (collateral) is the backup, never the plan: it protects depositors' money if the repayment source fails. And it must be proportionate — the financed asset plus a personal guarantee fits a small equipment loan.

client.name: Noura's Flower Studio
client.profile: Supplies flowers for weddings and corporate events. Approved yesterday for her first small facility — today you're processing it.

request: "I got the approval — wonderful! But now your operations team wants my trade license, my signature card, some 'board resolution'... why all this paper? The loan is approved, isn't it? Just send the money!"

figures.label: Status
figures.value: Approved — but not yet paid out

ratios.label: Why process matters
ratios.value: Approval decides IF; process makes it SAFE
ratios.hint: The credit decision says the loan makes sense. The process — checking licenses, signatures, documents, in the right order — makes sure the money goes to the right legal person, under an enforceable agreement. Skip it, and even a good loan becomes a bad one.

ratios.label: What the documents prove
ratios.hint: Trade license: the business legally exists. Signature card: the person signing is really her. Each paper answers one question that matters if anything is ever disputed.

decisions.prompt: What do you tell Noura about 'all this paper'?

options.label: Each document answers one question — that the business is real, the signer is really you, the agreement will hold. It protects you as much as us
options.feedback: Exactly right — and clients accept process happily when someone explains what each paper is FOR. An enforceable agreement protects both sides of it.

options.label: Skip the checks this once — she's clearly genuine
options.feedback: 'Clearly genuine' is what everyone looks like until the one time they aren't. Process exists precisely because exceptions can't be spotted by feel.

options.label: Honestly, it's bureaucracy — every bank suffers from it
options.feedback: Apologising for the process teaches clients to resent it. The process is the product: it's why a bank's agreements actually hold.

options.label: Pay first, collect papers later this week
options.feedback: Money first, checks later means the checks can no longer change anything. Order is the whole point: documents, then signatures, then money.

decisions.prompt: Her file arrives. Which item must be fixed BEFORE any money moves?

options.label: Her trade license expired last month
options.feedback: Caught it. An expired license means the business isn't currently in legal good standing — renew first, then proceed. This exact check protects every facility the bank ever books.

options.label: Her shop's Instagram handle isn't in the file
options.feedback: Marketing details are not legal requirements. Don't pad the process with theatre — it breeds contempt for the checks that matter.

options.label: The file is only 9 pages — make it look thicker
options.feedback: Thickness is not compliance. A complete thin file beats a padded thick one every day.

options.label: Nothing — approved means approved
options.feedback: Look again at the license date. Approval was yesterday's decision; today's job is making it safe to act on.

plantedError.prompt: Operations runs the final pre-payment check on Noura's file. Review it — anything wrong?
exhibit: Trade license No. 41207 — valid until 9 May 2026

options.label: The trade license expired on 9 May — last month
options.feedback: Well spotted. The license must be renewed before any payout — an agreement with a business that isn't in legal good standing may not hold.

options.label: The approval memo shouldn't be in the file
options.feedback: The approval memo is the file's foundation — it absolutely belongs there.

options.label: Nothing — release the funds
options.feedback: Check the license dates again: valid until 9 May, and today is 11 June.

learn: Approval decides IF the bank lends; the process makes it SAFE: license, signatures and documents — in the right order, before money moves. Each paper answers one question that matters when things go wrong.

client.name: Two applicants, one afternoon
client.profile: Your mentor slides two thin files across the desk. 'Both want KD 25,000 for a year. Read the numbers, tell me which one you'd back — and why. This is the whole job in miniature.'

request: "File A: Salem's Spices — sales KD 90,000, profit KD 14,000, no debts, in business 8 years. File B: FastTrend Kiosk — sales KD 200,000, LOSS of KD 9,000, already owes KD 40,000 elsewhere, open 14 months. FastTrend's owner drives a beautiful car and promises 'sales will triple soon'. Which file gets your recommendation?"

ratios.label: Profit vs sales
ratios.hint: FastTrend SELLS more than Salem — but loses money doing it. Profit is what's left after costs; a loss means every month makes the hole deeper. Repayment comes from profit, never from sales alone.

ratios.label: Existing debt
ratios.value: B already owes nearly 3× what it's asking
ratios.hint: New lenders stand at the back of the queue. If KD 40,000 of older debt is already straining a loss-making kiosk, our KD 25,000 would be fuel on a fire.

decisions.prompt: Which file do you recommend — and on what basis?

options.label: Salem's Spices — profitable, debt-free, proven over 8 years: the numbers can repay
options.feedback: That's the job: the loan goes to the business whose numbers can carry it home. Modest and profitable beats big and bleeding — every time.

options.label: FastTrend — bigger sales, bigger energy, sales will triple
options.feedback: Sales without profit are motion without progress, and 'will triple soon' is a wish, not a repayment source. The KD 40,000 already owed would swallow our money first.

options.label: Both — split KD 12,500 each, diversify
options.feedback: Half a bad loan is still a bad loan. Diversification means many GOOD risks, not a blend of good and bad.

options.label: Neither — both are too small to bother with
options.feedback: Small, profitable, loyal clients like Salem are the bedrock of a bank. Today's KD 25,000 borrower is next decade's KD 2,500,000 relationship.

decisions.prompt: Maryam nods. 'Last question: the car, the confidence, the big talk — what do they count for?'

options.label: Nothing by themselves — character matters, but the numbers must agree before charm gets a vote
options.feedback: Welcome to banking. Listen to people, like people, believe in people — and lend to the ones whose numbers agree. You'll meet this exact temptation, in bigger suits, for the rest of your career.

options.label: A lot — successful-looking people are usually successful
options.feedback: The most expensive sentence in finance. Looking successful is cheap; BEING profitable shows up only in the numbers — which is why we read them.

options.label: The car could be extra security — ask him to pledge it
options.feedback: Creative, but you'd be decorating a loan that's wrong at its core. No security fixes a missing repayment source — remember Abu Salem's first lesson.

options.label: Avoid confident people — confidence means hiding something
options.feedback: Cynicism is just gullibility pointing the other way. Confidence is fine; unsupported confidence is the flag.

learn: Repayment comes from profit, not sales, and never from charm: a modest profitable business beats a big loss-making one. Read the numbers first; let character confirm them — not replace them.
